title: Alcaraz Smiles Through 3:34 AM Loss, Calls for Schedule Change
summary:
Most players would not walk away smiling after their US Open title defense ended at 3:34 a.m. after five intense sets. Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.

After his loss to Ben Shelton — a match that lasted four hours and 28 minutes — the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin. Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament in over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day. He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling," he said.

The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1 a.m. in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2 a.m.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late. "The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed. I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11 p.m. or whatever would be better."

Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury. Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy."

He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September. The team tournament pits Europe — captained by Yannick Noah — against a United States team overseen by Andre Agassi.

"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said. "We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well."
why_it_matters: The debate over 3 a.m. finishes is really about who sport is built for — broadcasters and ticket sales, or the players whose bodies and careers are on the line — and it mirrors other industries where young workers are asking for limits on how far schedules can stretch them.

background_read: Flushing Meadows (the public park in Queens, New York, where the US Open has been played since 1978) hosts the last of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments, and its showpiece is Arthur Ashe Stadium — the largest tennis stadium in the world, named after Arthur Ashe (the American champion who became the first Black man to win a Grand Slam singles title).

Because the US Open sells separate night sessions in that stadium, play often runs past midnight, and players and commentators have complained for years that finishing at two or three in the morning hurts recovery and creates unfair conditions for whoever must play again the next day.

The Laver Cup (a team competition named after Rod Laver, the Australian who twice won all four major titles in a single year) is unusual in tennis because players who normally compete as individuals sit courtside together, led by former greats such as Andre Agassi (an American who won eight Grand Slam singles titles) and Yannick Noah (a French champion who later became a pop singer).
Injury is a constant theme in the modern game: the calendar is long, the hard courts are punishing, and top players can lose months of a season at a time.

perspectives.description: Alcaraz treats the loss as a sign of progress rather than a disaster, because he is back competing after months of pain. His call for an 11 p.m. cut-off focuses attention on recovery time, and his plan to skip some events shows a player putting long-term health above short-term ranking points.

Organisers and television partners argue that night sessions draw the biggest global audiences and the money that pays prize funds. Fixing a hard finish time, they warn, could mean cancelling or moving matches, disappointing fans who bought tickets for a specific session.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — analysts of the tennis calendar
perspectives.description: Analysts note that this is a structural problem, not a one-off: a crowded calendar, hard courts and long five-set matches pile up, and the biggest names are increasingly injured at the same time. Late finishes have been debated for years without a permanent fix.

Possible fixes include earlier starts, fewer matches on the main court each day, or a rule that no match may begin after a set hour. If top players keep missing Slams with injuries, pressure from sponsors and fans may finally force the sport to shorten its season.
